name: Shelta
catalog_citation: Macalister, R.A.S. 1937. The Secret Languages of Ireland. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. (archive.org item the-secret-languages-of-ireland_202307, scanned full text)
catalog_locator: p. 165 (accent statement, in the section on word-formation from Irish); p. 157 (transcription convention for accent in the vocabulary)
catalog_quote: vowel is lengthened, as in kfit’i< 4cwid: in others it is shortened, as is the second vowel of lak(@)r < /4illifir. This is evidently in most cases a result of accent-shift, as the accent in Shelta appears to be thrown almost universally on to the first syllable of the word, irrespective of the accentuation of the corresponding Irish word. This is another indication of a predominating English infiuence. ... [p. 157:] The accentuation of syllables is denoted (with an acute accent on the vowel) only when it falls otherwise than on the first syllable.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: both deciding quotations are verbatim in the held Macalister 1937 scanned text and PDF at the stated pages (p.165 accent statement; p.157 transcription convention). The coding (fixed initial stress, exceptions lexically marked) follows directly from the author's explicit generalization plus his marking convention. Source quality: Macalister 1937 is old and philological (built on 1890s collections), but it remains the only full structural description of Shelta; the later literature I could identify from Crossref, archive.org and Wikipedia's bibliography (Hancock 1984, Grant 1994, Binchy 1994, Kirk & O Baoill 2002, Browne 2004, Rieder 2018, Clancy 2023) is sociolinguistic/mixed-language in orientation and none is a phonology or instrumental study; Glottolog's descriptive list for shel1236 is largely mislinked noise. Since Shelta's grammatical and phonological frame is (Hiberno-)En
